newsitem.title: USA: Decision expected soon in GE vs. reinsurers case.
newsitem.headline: Decision expected soon in GE vs. reinsurers case.

text.p: A Massachusetts Supreme Court justice is expected to rule in the next few weeks in a closely watched case which pits General Electric Co against some of the world's biggest reinsurers.

At issue is whether the Massachusetts insurance commissioner will be appointed U.S. receiver of Electric Mutual Liability Insurance Company Ltd (EMLICO), which filed a petition for voluntary winding up shortly after moving to Bermuda from Massachusetts in 1995.
The decision would resolve the controversy surrounding EMLICO's liquidation and have a bearing on how soon the claims of EMLICO's 400 reinsurers would be resolved.

The case is significant because it may have some bearing on to what degree insurers are allowed to restructure themselves in the face of massive environmental claims, legal sources said. EMLICO's sole policyholder was Connecticut-based General Electric, which is potentially at risk for up to $2 billion in environmental and asbestos-related claims.

EMLICO's reinsurers, including Lloyd's of London, Kemper Insurance Co's Kemper Reinsurance Co and Hannover Ruckversicherungs AG, claim that EMLICO moved to Bermuda simply to take advantage of the country's more favorable insolvency laws.

They allege that Bermuda law allowed GE to hand-pick EMLICO's liquidators and effectively control them, enabling GE to have its environmental and asbestos claims against EMLICO approved by the liquidators in an inflated amount.

Also siding with the reinsurers is the Center for Insurance Research, a Cambridge, Mass.-based consumer group which claims that a settlement agreement worked out between General Electric, EMLICO and the Massachusetts insurance commissioner in March of this year was not in the public interest. The consumer group contends that the commissioner, by agreeing to leave EMLICO in Bermuda, was trying to sweep the matter under the rug to avoid embarrassment.
On the other side are GE, EMLICO, its liquidators, and regulators, who argue that the reinsurers are trying to shirk their contractual duty to pay up on claims.
The case is important because there are hundreds of millions of dollars worth of environmental claims pending in courts around the country, a GE spokesperson said.

"The reinsurance industry has a lot at stake in how these claims are ultimately decided," said Larry Rasky, a public relations consultant for GE. "There are an awful lot of environmental claims, besides GE's, waiting for disposition."

Rasky said reinsurers have been trying to avoid accepting liability on environmental damages for many years. "But until now, they haven't had to go up against someone with the resources of GE to fight them."
The reinsurers are trying to use the redomestication of EMLICO as "a smokescreen to further delay facing up to their claims," Rasky alleged.

However, the reinsurers insist they would pay any claims which were legitimate. They say GE is simply trying "to deflect attention from the serious and well-documented fraud claims raised by reinsurers," according to court documents filed by Hannover Re.

"Hannover Re is refusing to stand idly by while a politically well-connected corporation manipulates the regulatory process, abuses its insurance subsidiary and seeks unlawfully to force upon reinsurers its massive, uninsured liabilities for the damages it has caused by its polluting activities," Hannover Re said in the court documents.
The case has been in litigation since 1995.
So far, EMLICO and its liquidators have successfully thwarted reinsurers' efforts to have a full hearing on the fraud and redomestication issues.
Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court Justice John M. Greaney has been contemplating the decision since both sides presented final arguments on May 16.
